review.headline: A chaotic opening gives way to a decisive kingside counterattack

sections.text: Against the Nimzo-Larsen, you handled the center solidly before stumbling under early pressure. Facing 9.Qg4, you opted for 9...Kf7?? rather than castling with 9...O-O, leaving your king exposed. White snatched a pawn on c7, but quickly overextended by hunting material instead of completing development.

White made a fatal mistake on the back rank with 19.Bxc8??, completely ignoring the loose rook on h1. You capitalized immediately with 19...Qxh1+!, skewering the d1 king against the b1 knight and winning a whole rook to take full control of the game.

White's king was flushed out into the open, though you missed a direct mate with 24...Qf1+ and instead played 24...Rxc3+?. Despite the detour, you kept hunting the king. When White pinned your bishop with 36.Qc5??, you broke out with 36...Bxd4+!, executing a clean fork against king and queen that won the queen on move 37 and forced resignation.

review.turning_point: White blundered a full rook with 19.Bxc8??, allowing 19...Qxh1+! which transformed White's early initiative into a completely lost king hunt.
review.focus: Prioritize king safety in the opening; playing 9...Kf7?? instead of 9...O-O created self-inflicted danger when you were under attack.

review.headline: A winning piece up slips away in a final-move hallucination

sections.text: White essayed the aggressive Cochrane Gambit with 4.Nxf7?, forking your queen and rook on d8 and h8, but you gladly accepted the piece with 4...Kxf7!. After 8.e5?? dxe5! 9.Rxe5 Nbd7, you consolidated cleanly and held an extra bishop. However, 10...Qb6?? and 12...g6?? handed White attacking chances, though you defended resourcefully with 13...Kd8! to maintain your material edge.

In the middlegame, you took control of the open e-file with 21...Rxe1+ 22.Qxe1 Re8. You ran into trouble with 23...Bf4??, but White failed to punish it with 24.Qd2??. You seized the opportunity with 24...Bxe3! 25.fxe3 Bf5, retaining a winning advantage. Later, you snapped off a passed pawn with 34...Qxc4! and comfortably neutralized White's central push.

Even after multiple trades, your extra piece kept you firmly in the driver's seat. White launched desperate checks, but your king found shelter on a7. With White's heavy pieces overextended, you were completely winning, but a sudden calculation blind spot brought the game to an abrupt end.

review.headline: A dominant endgame conversion undone only by the clock

sections.text: You seized an early pawn in the opening and applied pressure, setting up a pin on the c6-knight with 4.Bb5 and another on the f6-knight with 8.Bg5. However, after pushing 9.e5, you slipped with 10.Qd5, creating a pin against the d7-bishop but allowing 10...Nxg5, which cost a piece. Eskaks returned the favor immediately with 11...Be6, setting up a skewer against your queen and bishop. You punished it cleanly with 12.Nxe6!.

After 12...Qxd5, you missed the intermediate fork 13.Nxc7+ Kd7 14.Nxd5 and played 13.Bxd5 instead, though you remained ahead. When Black harassed your kingside with 15...Bh4, setting a pin along the e1-h4 diagonal, you responded accurately with 16.g3! to kick the bishop away and solidify your extra material.

From there, your technique was excellent. You traded down rooks, marched your king forward into Black's territory, and used your passed pawns to force Black to give up their remaining pieces. You promoted safely to a queen with 55.a8=Q and drove the lone black king into the corner, but unfortunately flagged on move 69.

review.turning_point: Black's blunder 11...Be6 allowed 12.Nxe6!, wiping out Black's opening advantage and handing you complete control of the game.
review.focus: Look for intermediate checks and captures before simple recaptures, as 13.Nxc7+ Kd7 would have won even more material on the spot than 13.Bxd5.

sections.text: Out of the Philidor Defense, play opened quickly. You created central tension and castled smoothly, but when White grabbed on d6 with 13.Qxd6, they used a pin on your knight against your queen. After trading into the middlegame, you doubled pressure down the e-file and won a piece back with 16...Rxe2, steering into an equal major-piece endgame.

Rooks were traded down to a single-rook endgame where both sides mobilized their passed pawns. White pushed their c-pawn, while you responded by rolling your kingside pawns forward with 31...f5 and 32...g4, setting up a decisive race.

The game reached maximum tension on move 34. White tried to halt your g-pawn with 34.Rc2, but that walked right into 34...Rxc6!. You gave up the rook to eliminate White's dangerous passed pawn and immediately pushed 35...g2, ensuring promotion and the win.

sections.text: You seized total control right out of the opening. White slipped with 10.Qd2, and you punished it immediately with 10...h6!, pushing their pieces backward. When they compounded the mistake with 11.Nxe5, you took the bishop on g5 with 11...Qxg5!, securing a decisive material advantage that carried smoothly into the endgame.

Your knight maneuvered aggressively to pick off pawns, winning material with 25...Nxh3 and 26...Nxf2. You maintained an evaluation above +5.0 into the late game, but as the position simplified, your piece coordination began to unravel. Instead of securing your rook with 52...Nd5+, you walked into trouble with 52...Kb3??, leaving your rook to be taken by 53.Kxf4 and letting White back into an equal ending.

Even after losing the rook, you held a theoretical draw in the knight-versus-rook endgame. Precision was essential with so little material left. Moving 73...Kd4?? stepped onto the same file as your knight, allowing 74.Rd6+ to attack both pieces and force the loss of your knight.

review.turning_point: The decisive shift came on 52...Kb3??, which left your rook to be captured on 53.Kxf4 and threw away a completely winning position.
review.focus: Keep tabs on undefended pieces before launching king raids in the endgame, as missing White's threat on 52...Kb3 cost you a full rook.

review.headline: A swift queen raid punishes uncastled king

sections.text: You faced an Open Sicilian where Black gave up central control early by trading knights with 4...Nxd4. After 6...e5 kicked your queen, 7.Qd1 was a slight retreat, though it maintained a pin on d6 against the black queen. You kept developing naturally with 8.Bc4 and 9.O-O while Black fell behind on king safety.

sections.text: After trades on d5, 13.exd5 was a mild inaccuracy that gave up some queen activity, but Black didn't challenge your center. Instead, Black left their king vulnerable with 14...Be7. You immediately jumped on the mistake with 15.Qb5+!, forcing 15...Kd8 and preventing Black from ever castling.

Your queen tore through Black's queenside, picking up pawns with 16.Qxb7 and 17.Qxa7. Desperate for counterplay, Black grabbed a poisoned pawn with 18...Qxb2, leaving their queen entirely undefended. You cleanly snapped it off with 19.Qxb2!, forcing an immediate resignation.

review.turning_point: Black's passive 14...Be7 allowed 15.Qb5+!, fatally trapping Black's king in the center and dismantling their queenside.
review.focus: Consider keeping your queen active on dominant central squares instead of retreating all the way home, as seen on 7.Qd1.

sections.text: You handled the opening with great maturity against the English Opening. After 3.cxd5 exd5, the symmetrical pawn structure called for steady, harmonious development. You placed your rooks actively on the central files with 16...Rad8 and 17...Rfe8, and after the trade on f6 and 19...Rxe3 20.fxe3 gxf6, your pieces were actively eyeing White's weakened e3-pawn.

White tried to push your bishop away with 22.b4??, but this walked straight into your pressure against e3. You punished it immediately with 22...Qxe3+!. White compounded the mistake with 23.Qxe3?? into the pin on the c5-g1 diagonal, walking directly into your fork with 23...Bxe3+! against the king on g1 and the rook on c1.

review.headline: A sharp Philidor that turned on a single tactical oversight

sections.text: You chose the Nimzowitsch Variation of the Philidor Defense, quickly active after 4...Nxe4 and 5...Bxd6. When White pinned your knight with 6.Qe2, you broke the pin with 6...Qe7 and soon castled. White tried to kick your piece with 8.f3, which was a huge blunder.

Here you had an immediate knockout: 8...Qh4+ would have won quickly. Instead, you chose 8...Nf6, creating a discovered attack on White's queen, but it allowed queen trades with 9.Qxe7 Bxe7 and let White off the hook. After 10...Be6? and 13...Nd5?, you let White keep things close.

Your move 13...Nd5 uncorked a discovered attack on White's bishop on g5. White completely missed the threat and played 14.Nc3, allowing you to win a piece on the spot with 14...Bxg5!. From there, you cleaned up the extra material with 16...Bxf4, kept active bishops, and forced White to resign.

review.turning_point: White's blunder 14.Nc3 overlooked your attack on their dark-squared bishop, letting you grab a full minor piece with 14...Bxg5! and take total control.
review.focus: Look for forcing attacking moves against an uncastled king before retreating; on 8...Nf6, you missed the crushing check 8...Qh4+.

Instead of falling into trouble, you cleanly defused the threat with 24...Nxd5!, kicking off a mass trade of minor pieces that simplified into a winning position.

Both sides traded mutual oversights around your hanging bishop, starting with 28...Qb6?? setting up a pin along the a7-g1 diagonal. White neglected to take the piece with 29.Rab1?? and again with 31.Kh1??. You immediately seized the opportunity with 31...Bd6!, swinging your dark-squared bishop into a lethal battery toward White's king.
